title: Playing
hookLine: hide-and-seek, a monk in a field all night, and a boy under a rose-apple tree
tomorrow: what do you say to a mother carrying her child from house to house?

cards: Grown-ups who play hide-and-seek usually hide badly on purpose, so the game ends and the phone can come back out. Ryokan hid well. He was a Zen monk and poet in Japan, and tradition says the village children loved him.
One evening, the story goes, he folded himself into a field to hide. Dusk came. The children forgot him and went home to dinner.
He stayed. In the morning a farmer found him crouched there and asked what on earth he was doing. Hush, he said.

teach.h: A BALL WRAPPED IN BRIGHT THREAD.
teach.b: Ryokan's poems talk about this life: begging in the villages, and the children who come running, and the hand-ball game, temari, a ball wrapped in bright thread, bounced and counted out in rhymes.
A monk, counting bounces with a crowd of kids, and calling it a good day. That sounds like a break from practice. The suttas hint it might be the practice.

teach.h: A BOY UNDER A ROSE-APPLE TREE.
teach.b: In one, the Buddha remembers being a boy, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father worked nearby. His mind settled into a quiet, bright happiness.
Years later, worn out by harsh austerities, the memory comes back, and he asks himself a question: why am I afraid of this happiness? It has nothing to do with craving.
He decides he isn't afraid of it, and that memory points him toward the way he finally walks. Joy has a name in the teaching, piti, and it's counted among the qualities that lead to awakening.
So the playing isn't a pause in the path. A ball in the hand, a rhyme, a child's laugh, and a mind fully in it: that's attention, and it's glad.
Ryokan stayed in the field because the game was real. Not to make a point, and not to teach anyone a lesson. He was simply still playing.

how: Ryokan is remembered in Japan through his poems and stories about playing temari and hide-and-seek with village children; some Buddhist teachers point to him when they talk about joy as part of practice.

o: a way to keep children quiet while adults meditate
time off from the path, allowed only after practice
a game given full, glad attention, as part of the path

games.q: joy on the path — tap the pairs.
p: a Zen monk who played with village kids
a hand-ball wrapped in bright thread
where the boy's mind grew bright and still
joy, a quality on the way to awakening

s: in the Buddhist path, joy is a distraction to be pushed away
joy, piti, is counted among the qualities that lead to awakening.
the Buddha asked himself why he was afraid of a happiness free of craving
remembering the rose-apple tree, he decided he wasn't afraid of it.

games.q: your little sister begs you to play the same card game again. you're tired and half-watching your phone. what would Ryokan's way look like?
o: say no; rest is the mindful choice when you're this tired.
play one round with the phone face down, all the way in.
keep playing while scrolling; she won't know the difference.
games.why: the point isn't how long you play but how fully. Ryokan stayed in the field because the game was real to him.

practice: Find something soft you can toss: a balled-up sock, an orange, a pair of gloves. Pass it slowly from hand to hand, and feel each landing: the weight, the small slap, the catch, the tiny pause at the top of the arc.
If a child is nearby, toss it to them instead and let them set the rules.

wordCard.voice: Playing: joy with full attention, the kind Ryokan found with the village kids, and the Buddha remembered from a childhood afternoon.

orig.note: Pali: joy, gladness; counted among the qualities that lead to awakening.

carryVoice: For your pocket today: play, and mean it while you do. Ten of eleven, nearly through family.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta: the childhood memory under the rose-apple tree; 'why am I afraid of that pleasure, which has nothing to do with sensual pleasures?')
Samyutta Nikaya 46 (the factors of awakening, including joy, piti)
